nodes.label: special relativity
nodes.description: Theory reconciling mechanics with Maxwellian electrodynamics through relativistic kinematics.

nodes.label: general relativity
nodes.description: Geometric theory of gravitation developed by Einstein between 1907 and 1915.

nodes.label: equivalence principle
nodes.description: Principle identifying local free-fall with inertial motion and motivating general relativity.

nodes.label: spacetime
nodes.description: Geometric framework in which space and time form a unified structure; Minkowski's reformulation was adopted by Einstein.

nodes.label: mass–energy equivalence
nodes.description: Equivalence of mass and energy associated with E = mc².

nodes.label: photoelectric effect
nodes.description: Phenomenon for which Einstein proposed quantized light energy and for which he received the Nobel Prize.

nodes.label: light quanta / photons
nodes.description: Einstein's proposal that light energy is exchanged in localized quanta; later called photons.

nodes.label: Brownian motion
nodes.description: Random motion of suspended particles explained as evidence for molecular/atomic reality.

nodes.label: statistical mechanics
nodes.description: Statistical description of matter and thermodynamic behavior.

nodes.label: thermodynamic fluctuations
nodes.description: Statistical variations in physical quantities such as density and energy.

nodes.label: critical opalescence
nodes.description: Milky appearance of a fluid near its critical point due to large density fluctuations scattering light.

nodes.label: quantum theory
nodes.description: Framework concerning discrete energy quanta and quantum phenomena to which Einstein made foundational contributions.

nodes.label: Bose–Einstein statistics
nodes.description: Statistics developed from Bose's counting method and Einstein's extension to particles/atoms.

nodes.label: Bose–Einstein condensate
nodes.description: Low-temperature collective state predicted in Einstein's work on Bose statistics.

nodes.label: wave–particle duality
nodes.description: Recognition that quantum entities such as light exhibit both wave-like and particle-like aspects.

nodes.label: matter waves
nodes.description: de Broglie's wave concept for matter, which Einstein supported and connected to quantization.

nodes.label: stimulated emission
nodes.description: Process introduced in Einstein's 1917 radiation work and foundational to masers and lasers.

nodes.label: spontaneous emission
nodes.description: Radiative process treated in Einstein's 1917 quantum theory of radiation.

nodes.label: Einstein coefficients
nodes.description: Statistical coefficients governing absorption, spontaneous emission, and stimulated emission.

nodes.label: Einstein solid
nodes.description: Model treating lattice atoms as independent quantized harmonic oscillators.

nodes.label: zero-point energy
nodes.description: Minimum energy associated with quantized systems, investigated by Einstein and Otto Stern.

nodes.label: gravitational waves
nodes.description: Propagating ripples in spacetime curvature predicted by general relativity.

nodes.label: gravitational lensing
nodes.description: Deflection of light by gravitating bodies predicted by Einstein's gravitational theory.

nodes.label: gravitational redshift
nodes.description: Frequency shift associated with gravitational fields predicted in Einstein's development of relativity.

nodes.label: gravitational time dilation
nodes.description: Difference in clock rates associated with gravitational potential.

nodes.label: Einstein field equations
nodes.description: Field equations relating spacetime geometry to matter/energy in general relativity.

nodes.label: cosmological constant
nodes.description: Term introduced by Einstein into the gravitational field equations in 1917 in an attempt to obtain a static universe.

nodes.label: Einstein static universe
nodes.description: Static cosmological model arising from Einstein's 1917 application of general relativity.

nodes.label: Friedmann–Einstein universe
nodes.description: Dynamic cosmological model proposed by Einstein after the recession of galaxies became accepted.

nodes.label: Einstein–de Sitter universe
nodes.description: Dynamic cosmological model developed by Einstein and de Sitter.

source_claims.claim: The source identifies Einstein's life dates, education, major known contributions, doctoral thesis, advisors, fields, and affiliations.

Einstein is presented as a German-born theoretical physicist best known for relativity, with major contributions to quantum theory; the source highlights 1905, general relativity, cosmology, radiation, Bose–Einstein statistics, quantum objections, and unified field theory.
The source traces Einstein's childhood, compass/electromagnetism fascination, self-directed mathematics, Kant, Aarau education, ETH studies, and friendship with Marcel Grossmann and Mileva Marić.
The patent office work and Olympia Academy discussions are presented as contexts for Einstein's thought experiments and intellectual influences.
The source describes Einstein's early papers and the four 1905 annus mirabilis papers.
The source traces Einstein's European academic career, ETH, Prague, Berlin, the Prussian Academy, Kaiser Wilhelm Institute, and Nobel recognition.
The source describes the development and 1919 observational test of general relativity's light-deflection prediction.
The source describes Einstein's emergence as a global scientific celebrity and his international travels and intellectual debates.
The source describes Einstein's membership in the League of Nations intellectual cooperation committee.
The source describes Einstein's U.S. visits, Caltech research, pacifism, and relationship with Charlie Chaplin.
The source describes Nazi persecution, Einstein's renunciation of German citizenship, refugee status, advocacy for displaced scientists, and permanent move to the Institute for Advanced Study.
The source describes Einstein and Szilárd's warning to Roosevelt about German atomic-bomb research, Einstein's later regret, and his anti-nuclear advocacy.
The source describes Einstein's U.S. citizenship and civil-rights advocacy, including the NAACP, W. E. B. Du Bois, Lincoln University, and Marian Anderson.
The source describes Einstein's socialism, world-government advocacy, pacifism, relationship with Gandhi, Zionism, Hebrew University, and refusal of Israel's presidency.
The source describes Einstein's philosophical/religious views, humanism, vegetarianism, and lifelong engagement with violin and chamber music.
The source describes Einstein's final illness, death, cremation, brain preservation, memorialization, and archival bequest.

historical_timeline.description: Einstein born in Ulm in the Kingdom of Württemberg.
Einstein moved to Switzerland and later renounced Württemberg citizenship.
Graduated from the Swiss federal polytechnic teaching diploma program.
Secured permanent work at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.
Published four foundational papers on light quanta, Brownian motion, special relativity, and mass–energy equivalence.
Completed the general theory and published the Einstein field equations.
Applied GR to cosmology and published quantum theory of radiation with stimulated emission.
Eddington's observations supported the predicted gravitational deflection of light.
Received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1922, for the photoelectric effect.
Received Bose's statistical model and developed Bose–Einstein statistics.
Decided not to return to Nazi Germany and moved permanently toward the United States.
Published EPR and particle-problem work with collaborators.
Published On the Generalized Theory of Gravitation.
Died in Princeton after continuing to work; signed the Russell–Einstein Manifesto shortly before death.

semantic_distinctions.explanation: Matter is treated as a substance/category or physical content, whereas mass is a quantitative property of matter or systems; the source explicitly warns that historical definitions sometimes conflate them.
E = mc² establishes equivalence between mass and energy, but the source distinguishes energy and force-mediating particles from what is conventionally called matter.
Einstein's work treats photons and matter using quantum concepts rather than assuming classical localized objects with ordinary trajectories.
Special relativity treats inertial frames and relativistic kinematics; general relativity extends the framework to gravitation and accelerated motion through spacetime geometry.
Einstein first introduced the cosmological constant to permit a static universe, then abandoned that model after evidence for galaxy recession.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Einstein's quantum contributions vs quantum objections
semantic_distinctions.explanation: Einstein was foundational to quantum theory but later rejected the claim that quantum randomness was fundamental or that standard quantum mechanics was complete.
EPR posed a completeness/realism challenge; Bell later derived experimentally testable constraints on local hidden-variable theories.
The source treats Entwurf as a real stage in Einstein's path to general relativity; abandonment is part of the theory-development history.
Einstein pursued geometric unification, but the source states the program did not incorporate strong and weak nuclear forces.
The Nobel Prize and eclipse reporting are distinct mechanisms of recognition; the latter made Einstein a global public icon.
Einstein's warning to Roosevelt created a documented tension with his pacifism, which he later reflected on critically.
Einstein's scientific work and his positions on realism, determinism, completeness, religion, and humanism are related but not identical domains.

misconceptions.correction: The source documents major contributions to statistical mechanics, Brownian motion, quantum theory, radiation, Bose–Einstein statistics, cosmology, and magnetization experiments in addition to relativity.

misconceptions.misconception: Einstein opposed quantum theory from the beginning
misconceptions.correction: Einstein made foundational contributions to quantum theory, including light quanta, quantum radiation, Bose–Einstein statistics, and matter-wave support; his later objections concerned interpretation and completeness.

misconceptions.misconception: E = mc² was Einstein's only important 1905 result
misconceptions.correction: The source identifies four major 1905 papers, with photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and mass–energy equivalence each contributing separately.

misconceptions.misconception: General relativity appeared fully formed in 1915
misconceptions.correction: The source traces a development from the 1907 equivalence principle through 1911 light deflection, 1913 geometric work, the Entwurf period, and completion in 1915.

misconceptions.misconception: Einstein's later work was uniformly successful
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly describes unsuccessful investigations and an unsuccessful unified-field program, as well as abandoned cosmological and gravitational approaches.
The source presents EPR as an argument challenging completeness; later Bell analysis transformed the issue into constraints on local hidden-variable explanations.

misconceptions.misconception: Einstein's science can be separated completely from philosophy
misconceptions.correction: The source connects his scientific reasoning with questions of realism, determinism, quantum completeness, epistemology, and his broader philosophical outlook.
